title: Unwritten signs do not imply unwritten saving dogmas — the same limit cuts both ways
source_text: VII. Porro quaenam est ista consequentia? Multa signa fecit Christus quae scripta non fuerunt, ergo sunt multa dogmata ad salutem necessaria quae sacra Scriptura comprehensa non sunt. Annon potius inde debemus concludere, quod quemadmodum Christus multa quidem signa fecit, quae in Scriptura sacra non memorantur, attamen de signis & miraculis ejus ex traditione nihil certi haberi potest, sed tantum ex Scriptura sacra: Ita quoque de Christi verbis atque doctrina nihil certum atque exploratum, nisi ex eadem Scriptura habemus. Ac praeterea, quod sicut de suis factis Christus tantum scribi voluit, quantum ad salutarem ejus notitiam satis est, ita quoque de suis verbis atque doctrina tantum scriptis mandari curavit, quantum ipsi ad fidem atque salutem nostram sufficere visum est.
pass_a_gloss: Further, what kind of consequence is that? Christ performed many signs which were not written, therefore there are many dogmas necessary to salvation which are not comprehended in sacred Scripture. Should we not rather conclude from that, that just as Christ indeed performed many signs which are not mentioned in sacred Scripture, yet concerning his signs and miracles nothing certain can be had from tradition, but only from sacred Scripture: so also concerning the words and doctrine of Christ we have nothing certain and ascertained except from the same Scripture. And besides, that just as concerning his deeds Christ wished only so much to be written as is enough for saving knowledge of him, so also concerning his words and doctrine he took care that only so much be committed to writing as seemed to him to suffice for our faith and salvation.
pass_b_english: Rome consequence fails: unwritten signs do not prove unwritten saving dogmas.
Better inference: even miracles are certain only from Scripture, not tradition.
Same for words and doctrine — certainty stays in Scripture.
Christ measured both deeds and teaching to what suffices for saving knowledge.
